title: In-situ Adjoint Wave Control in Reconfigurable Non-Hermitian Nonlinear Systems
authors: John Guillamon, William Tuxbury, Cheng-Zhen Wang, Owen Miller, Zin Lin, Tsampikos Kottos
abstract: Complex multipath environments are usually avoided in wave-based information processing because repeated scattering creates many interfering propagation paths, obscuring controllability and generating extreme sensitivity to perturbations. The addition of nonlinear mechanisms fundamentally alters the wave-control landscape by breaking the superposition principle that underpins most wave-management strategies. Here, we show that these two apparent impediments -- multipath complexity and nonlinearity -- can instead be harnessed as key resources for physical optimization. We demonstrate an in-situ adjoint optimization protocol in a wave-chaotic platform incorporating a single localized nonlinear defect, in which the system itself performs both the forward and the adjoint propagations required for gradient evaluation. Recurrent multipath returns repeatedly expose the wave to the defect, producing from a minimal hardware a rich nonlinear input-output map with many pathway-mediated degrees of freedom. At the same time, a suitable adjoint excitation enables direct extraction of the sensitivities from measurements alone, without a digital twin or conventional numerical backpropagation. We experimentally validate the protocol on a minimal nonlinear multipath platform composed of incommensurate coaxial cables connected via T-junctions, one of which hosts a diode-loaded cavity. Our approach opens a route to adaptive wireless communications, imaging and analog intelligence in complex, partially unknown environments where conventional modeling is impractical.
summary: This work introduces an In-situ Adjoint Optimization Protocol (iNAP) to enable real-time gradient-based optimization in complex nonlinear wave systems. By physically performing both forward and adjoint propagations on hardware, the method allows researchers to adaptively control devices like wireless communications components despite inherent multipath complexity and nonlinearity. This bypasses major computational bottlenecks associated with traditional system modeling.
main_problem: The research aims to overcome limitations in wave control by harnessing multipath complexity and nonlinearity, which are typically seen as impediments.
main_result: They successfully demonstrate an in-situ adjoint optimization protocol (iNAP) that allows for real-time gradient calculation in complex nonlinear physical systems without needing digital twins or conventional backpropagation.
method: The core method is the In-situ Adjoint Optimization Protocol (iNAP), which involves sequential forward and adjoint measurements performed directly on the physical hardware to calculate parameter sensitivities.
model_or_system: The system utilizes a minimal platform composed of incommensurate coaxial cables forming a wave-chaotic multipath network, incorporating a single localized nonlinear defect. The analysis also details deriving a self-consistency equation for the resonator intensity by integrating out linear graph degrees of freedom.
key_observables: Objective function gradient sensitivities ($\partial g / \partial p$), field measurements ($\Psi$, $\zeta$), and the resonant intensity ($y$).
important_parameters: The nonlinearity strength, input power levels (e.g., -50 to 10 dBm), and system parameters $p$.
main_assumptions: For iNAP, a crucial assumption is enforcing field invariance under phase conjugation at the nonlinear defect to ensure adjoint dynamics match hardware emulation. For modeling, invertibility of the linear graph matrix ($\mathbf{A}^{-1}_g$) is assumed.

paper_structure: The paper progresses from establishing the theoretical need to harness nonlinearity/multipath, detailing the iNAP protocol using adjoint fields in hardware (Chunk 1 & 2), deriving a compact scalar self-consistency equation by integrating out linear graph modes (Chunk 3), and finally characterizing a physical nonlinear vertex using this framework (Chunk 4).
why_interesting: The development of an *in-situ* optimization protocol that bypasses the need for full system modeling or digital twins is highly relevant to quantum optics and open quantum systems, as it provides a pathway for adaptive control in complex, noisy physical implementations.
